articles.text: Most residents know that the venerable Piedmont Community Pool had exceeded its useful life. It no longer served the needs of our community and was terribly dated. For many years the community reviewed, discussed and debated the issue of the aged community pool. As Mayor and with support of the City Council, I believed it was important that the community make the decision about the future of the Piedmont Community Pool. They made that decision decisively in November 2020 and told the City Council to move forward on a new aquatic facility. Many thought Measure UU could not pass; I believed that if any community could support such a measure, it would be Piedmont. The proposed pool will serve the varied aquatic and recreational needs of the Piedmont Community. As well, it will become a great venue for community and family events. The project fulfills all the requirements that the city and community asked for in a new pool facility. It will provide space for the community to gather and greatly enhanced recreational opportunities. Piedmont USD aquatics will also greatly benefit. The swimming and water polo programs are very successful and continually growing. Student-athletes in the aquatics programs deserve to have a facility that serves the programs as all other sports teams do. Along with the newly renovated Corey Reich Tennis Center, the Piedmont Center for the Arts and the new performance center at Piedmont High School, the Community Pool will be a great addition that enhances our community. The City Council moved quickly on the project. Bonds were issued at low interest rates. Plans were finalized and an outstanding architect and project management team assembled. That’s the good news. The cost environment, however, has been the bad news. Inflation is not news to any of us and it has led to increased costs. These increased costs are not cost overruns: they are the result of cumulative increases in materials and labor that have impacted projects across the state. This has created a funding gap of $2.1 million. This gap represents the amenities and capacity of the pool as currently proposed and those of a scaled-back version; a multi-purpose activity room is an example that would need to be cut. Our community deserves the best facility we can build: Piedmonters have and should expect the best. We need the community’s help to bridge the funding gap. The Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization is actively fundraising. Many of our neighbors have already donated. My family and I have pledged to support this effort. I hope you will consider making a donation to help build a great pool and community facility. It will serve us well for many decades to come. As with Measure UU, I’m confident that Piedmont can get this done. articles.text: The American Red Cross of Northern California needs special volunteers to deliver blood products to hospitals in local communities and provide the vital link between blood donors and patients who need blood products. Volunteers in the blood transportation specialist position have two important assignments — to transport blood from our blood collection sites to our labs throughout the region for testing and processing and to deliver blood products to hospitals in the area using a Red Cross-owned vehicle. WHAT DOES IT TAKE? These crucial volunteers will be asked to fill two to four shifts in their region each month, and the assignment usually taking about four hours to complete. The need for these transports may be scheduled during the day, in the evening, and on weekends. If you have a valid state driver’s license and at least three years of licensed driving experience, you can choose regular routes, stand-by emergency deliveries or both. This is a great volunteer opportunity for individuals, couples, friends or family members. Volunteers must be able to lift as much as 45 pounds. Training is provided by the Red Cross. Blood transportation specialists can schedule their own hours while helping patients in need. “It only takes a few hours each week to have an impact on someone’s life. When you join us, as a member of our Blood Transportation Team, you’ll serve as a critical link in getting blood donations to those who need them,” said Patty Montmorency, Blood Services Transportation Team Lead. “Training is free, but the blood you deliver is priceless.” Hear firsthand why others For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Community support for the Piedmont Community Pool project continues to grow with more families donating to ensure that key elements of the City’s plan for the new Pool Center are included in the project. The Piedmont Recreational Foundation (PRFO) has a target of raising $2.1 million. “We really appreciate the generosity of the Piedmont families who have donated to the Piedmont Community Pool Project Campaign. The success of this campaign is a tribute to our community’s commitment to our athletic and recreational facilities,” said PRFO President, Steve Collins. The funds raised by PRFO will help ensure key elements of the project will be included. This includes funds needed for the competitive-sized pool to be built at a regulation length and depth for water polo play and competitive swimming, a diving well with two diving boards, a scoreboard, timing system, sports lighting, and starting blocks and toe ledges. Funds could also cover three (3) standard-length lap lanes and a shallow area for play and swim lessons in the Activity Pool, and a poolside room for parties and gatherings. Community members who make a donation by December 31 will be included in the PRFO donor list published in local papers and will also be able to take advantage of 2022 tax deductions. Many companies offer end-of-year corporate matching, which can increase donor impact. For those who have not yet made their gift, remember that this is an instance where giving is more than its own reward! Every dollar contributed to the campaign directly benefits our community, student athletes, and our city. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host its Annual Holiday Luncheon at Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, this Friday, December 2. The cost is $40 for LWV members and $45 for guests. This year’s event will feature guest speaker Shannon Olivieri Hovis, Director of NARAL ProChoice California, who will discuss the role of California in the fight for reproductive rights after the Supreme Court’s recent Roe v. Wade decision. Hovis is a civil rights policy expert with fifteen years of experience in state and local government, classrooms, electoral campaigns, and political advocacy. While at NARAL, Hovis played a critical role on the California Future of Abortion Council, leading a legislative package of 16 bills in 2022, including a constitutional amendment to specifically enshrine the right to abortion and contraception in the California state Constitution. This year has been the worst year for reproductive freedom on record. In June, the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, ending the constitutional right to abortion and allowing states to enforce total bans on abortion. This decision eviscerated federal constitutional protections for abortion access, sending a clear and terrifying message to Americans: Freedom to determine if, when, and how to start or grow a family is now gone for many people across the country. Emboldened Shannon Olivieri Hovis, Director of NARAL Pro-Choice California, is the guest speaker at the Piedmont League of Women Voters Holiday Luncheon. by the Supreme Court decision, anti-choice lawmakers are racing to ban abortion in roughly half of the United States, with more than a dozen states already enforcing total or extreme bans. California is leading the fight to protect and expand access for all people. California has long played an outsized role in ensuring that all people can access the critical abortion care they need. Even before Roe v. Wade was overturned, California was home to one in four healthcare facilities in the country that provide abortion care. Now, as providers and clinics in states across the United States are forced to stop providing care, that percentage is increasing exponentially. pages.text: Wednesday, November 30, 2022 3 PRFO campaign for Community Pool in home stretch Community support for the Piedmont Community Pool project continues to grow with more families donating to ensure that key elements of the City’s plan for the new Pool Center are included in the project. The Piedmont Recreational Foundation (PRFO) has a target of raising $2.1 million. “We really appreciate the generosity of the Piedmont families who have donated to the Piedmont Community Pool Project Campaign. The success of this campaign is a tribute to our community’s commitment to our athletic and recreational facilities,” said PRFO President, Steve Collins. The funds raised by PRFO will help ensure key elements of the project will be included. This includes funds needed for the competitive-sized pool to be built at a regulation length and depth for water polo play and competitive swimming, a diving well with two diving boards, a scoreboard, timing system, sports lighting, and starting blocks and toe ledges. Funds could also cover three (3) standard-length lap lanes and a shallow area for play and swim lessons in the Activity Pool, and a poolside room for parties and gatherings. Community members who make a donation by December 31 will be included in the PRFO donor list published in local papers and will also be able to take advantage of 2022 tax deductions. Many companies offer end-of-year corporate matching, which can increase donor impact. For those who have not yet made their gift, remember that this is an instance where giving is more than its own reward! Every dollar contributed to the campaign directly benefits our community, student athletes, and our city. PRFO encourages the community to visit their website at PRFO.org to learn more about the project and to make a tax-deductible donation. articles.text: Starting on Tuesday, January 3, 2023, the City of Piedmont will offer rebates for the removal of existing gas appliances and replacement with certain electric appliances. Rebates will be available for single family and multi-family properties. Eligible low-income applicants may qualify for additional funding. Rebates will only be issued for existing buildings; new construction is not eligible for this program. Rebates can be applied to equipment and installation labor for projects applying for a Building Permit on or after January 3, 2023. Funding is limited and applications will be accepted until funding is exhausted. To learn more about qualification for the program, rebate amounts, and eligible electric appliances, please visit the following link: piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/planning___building/about_building_/rebates_and_incentives.

articles.text: The Curative COVID-19 testing station in the Community Hall parking lot will close permanently this week on Friday, December 3. The kiosk has provided over 11,000 tests in Piedmont since opening in November 2021. Originally open only two days per week, the site expanded to Monday through Friday service in January 2022. Demand has waned in recent months, and Curative has cited low use numbers as the reason for the site’s closure. “I’m proud that we’ve been able to provide this service to our community for over a year at no cost to the public,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Bringing a test site to our civic center last winter – when testing lines stretched around the block throughout the region – gave Piedmont residents a critical tool to navigate last year’s Omicron surge. Since then, the site has supported thousands of community members as they resumed elements of pre-pandemic life, including return to offices, attending large events, and enjoying long-delayed travel plans.” In contrast to when the site opened last year, COVID-19 tests are now widely available through many sources, including: • At-home tests: Home antigen tests are now easy to purchase at pharmacies and online. Additionally, the FDA has extended the expiration dates for many brands of home test kits, so tests you already have may still be good even if the printed expiration date has passed. • Public testing locations: Use the California Department of Public Health interactive map and search tool at myturn. ca.gov/testing to find local testing options. This site provides information about community clinics sponsored by Alameda County Public Health as well as sites run by private testing providers. The tool allows you to filter results to display only free testing sites, or locations that offer both testing and treatment.

articles.text: The Piedmont Beautification Foundation and City of Piedmont invite community members to kick off the holiday season with its annual tree lighting ceremony next Wednesday, December 7 at 7:00 p.m. in front of Piedmont Community Hall. This year’s event, called Lights Up!, represents an expansion of the celebration which dates to 1969. Longstanding traditions, including the illumination of the 80-foot redwood tree and a cappella serenades by Piedmont High School’s Troubadours will continue, enhanced by new additions intended to create a more inclusive and welcoming event that celebrates the diversity of Piedmont. In the depths of winter, celebrations centered around light are common to cultures across the globe. Building on this theme, Lights Up! will include new lighting around the park, the lighting of a menorah concurrently with the tree, and an activity hosted by Piedmont Girl Scouts inviting attendees to document how they plan to share their own inner light in the new year. A person named by the Make-A-Wish Foundation will flip the switch to turn on the lights on the redwood tree. Piedmont Scouts will serve warm apple cider and hot cocoa generously provided respectively by Piedmont Grocery and Heafey Baum Group. Chabad Oakland will add to the festivities this year with a latke station. Santa Claus will be available for photos inside Community Hall, and children are invited to write letters to Santa and deposit them in a special mailbox addressed to North Pole. Santa will read every letter. Children with special needs will be able to see Santa starting at 6:00pm. About PBF The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) obtains, maintains, installs, and removes the colorful LED lights that adorn the illuminated tree each year. Throughout the year, PBF partners with the City to provide research and funding for projects that increase safety, beauty, and function of Piedmont’s extensive and unique public facilities. Community members can support these efforts by donating at piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/donate. A donation to PBF this time of year provides an opportunity to extend warm wishes to friends and neighbors as part of the group’s 54th Annual Holiday Greeting Campaign by way of names of donors being listed in the Post and the Exedra. For questions contact Barbara Love at pbf.piedmont@gmail. com.
articles.title: Tree lighting ceremony, Lights Up!, set for December 7

articles.text: The Piedmont Neighbors & Newcomers Club will hold its annual Holiday Party at the home of Shonnon and Martin Schey on Friday, December 9, at 7 p.m. The event will feature catered appetizers and desserts, wine and beer, and special holiday cocktails. Festive or cocktail attire is appropriate. Shonnon, the President of the PNNC Board for four years, said that the holiday party will be the club’s first large event in three years. Despite a slower time, many new members have joined since 2019. “The best thing about PNNC is there’s something for everyone,” she said. “Many people who joined during the pandemic weren’t Piedmont newcomers at all, but locals interested in a deeper, broader connection with neighbors both new and old.” Concurrently with the re-introduction of larger events like the Holiday Party and their Supper Club (which currently boasts 135 members), Schey hopes to keep holding smaller gatherings like Girls’ and Guys’ Nights Out, children’s play groups, and book club gatherings. The Annual PNNC Holiday Party is open to PNNC members and non-members, but limited to adults only. Those interested may purchase a ticket for $50 until 9 a.m. on Thursday, December 1. and $60 after December 1 at piedmontpnnc.org/events-upcoming/2022/12/9/holiday-party.

articles.text: All those looking for viable, effective, trusted organizations to support as a part of your holiday season giving are invited to participate in Piedmont Community Church’s annual Alternative Gift Market on Sunday, December 11 from 11 a.m. to 12 noon. For nearly 20 years, Piedmont Church has sponsored this program as an opportunity for people to support local, national and international organizations dedicated to helping people in need. All groups are vetted by the church and chosen to maximize effect and result for all donations. All money received goes directly to the organizations you select. Gifts may be purchased in honor of a friend or relative, allowing donors to notify them with gift descriptions. Contributions are made at a separate station staffed by church volunteers receiving cash, checks, and credit cards. Complimentary coffee and pastries will be served. For an overview of the approximately 20 organizations involved, view the online catalog at PiedmontChurch.org/AGM where gifts can also be purchased. Everyone is encouraged to come in person to the Market. There is a feeling of excitement, a sense of spirituality and a shared joy of giving at this popular event. Visit PiedmontChurch.org/ AGM or contact the church at (510) 547-5700. Piedmont Community Church is located at 400 Highland Avenue.

articles.text: It’s the time of year when gift giving is top of mind, especially for parents searching for toy ideas for their tots. Since play is the foundation for robust learning, many parents are looking for toys that will be fun as well as infused with learning potential. How do we evaluate the quality of a toy in terms of a beneficial learning edge as well as the fun factor? What do we look for in a toy? We can look to the research for a few guiding principles. Regarding quantity, research shows that a bit less is best. For some children, the overload of all the play items can be overwhelming and distracting, causing the child to pick up one toy, drop it and move on. Regarding quality, research would have us remember the value of the simple “open-ended” toy which can be used in multiple ways. For example, hardwood blocks can be for building, or a make-believe car, or pretend food. Conversely, “closed-ended” toys (which consumers tend to gravitate toward when gift giving) tend to have a “right way” to play, and include such toys as a cash register, Mr. Potato Head, or Legos. Beyond these general principles of quantity and quality, what should be our toy buying guide? To foster problem solving, look to toys such as blocks, instruments or simple board games (or consider keys and containers with lids which you do not have to purchase). To tap into the child’s experimental tendencies, consider toys such as a sand or water table (or look to flashlights, colanders, or a whisk to use in the bath which you do not have to purchase). To encourage communication, doll houses and books are excellent choices (or introduce dress up or rhyming games for similar effects without a price tag). Cognitive development can be fun with toy items such as matching/memory and sorting picture cards, but can also be enjoyed with sorting of silverware, clothing or small household items using a muffin tin for a non-retail option. Creative kids will enjoy gifts of silly putty, paint or other art supplies (tape, paper towel rolls, paper plates and cotton balls can also be creative fun without additional purchases). Motor development can be enhanced with gifts such as puzzles, balls and shape sorters. And don’t forget that the same fun and developmental stimulation can be had with common kitchen items such as measuring cups, mixing bowls, plastic cups, etc. Regarding social/emotional based toys, dolls and puppets can’t be beat, and a mirror can do the trick for a no purchase option. Collaborative toys are always a good idea, such as a construction set or play kitchen. If you want to get the same effect without the specific toy purchase, the laundry basket, sheets and pillows can become a wonderful collaborative fort building experience. Have a wonderful gift-giving season. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. articles.text: Piedmont opened its season with a strong 73-35 victory over Marin Catholic. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team opened its season in a big way, bashing Marin Catholic 73-35 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, November 26. The victory comes against a Marin Catholic side that went 23-10 last season, advancing to the NCS Finals, and reaching the second round of the CIF State Tournament. The Wildcats lost just two seniors from last year’s team. “I thought we did pretty well with the game plan. The coaching staff had a great scouting report on Marin Catholic,” said assistant coach Shamaree Worley who was filling in for coach Ben Spencer out due to illness. “The kids executed well on what we wanted them to do. Our defense was pretty solid; we held them for nearly two points for an entire quarter. We moved well offensively as well, and nearly our entire roster scored,” said. Senior A.J. Harris led the way with 26 points and 10 rebounds, and junior Brit Burden had 19 points and nine rebounds. “Our leaders A.J. and Brit showed up big time with scoring, getting rebounds, and making sure the team is upbeat,” said Worley. Burden will be a major part of this year’s team after playing a smaller role last season. The Piedmont coaching staff has often praised Burden for his development over the offseason and has long expected him to become a focal point as their big man. “I believe that Brit can be a 20-10 guy for us in points and rebounds. We’re expecting a lot from him because we know what we’re getting from A.J. We need that second-punch coming from him. He’s a junior now and he already has next-level expectations of himself.” A.J. Harris scored 26 points and had 10 rebounds. Brit Burden had 19 points and pulled down nine rebounds. Staff Photos Piedmont led 21-10 by the end of the first quarter and 36-23 at halftime. From there, the Highlanders allowed just 12 second-half points by way of six points conceded in both the third and fourth quarters. PHS scored 22 points in the third to lead 58-29 by halftime and 15 in the fourth to win it 73-35. Piedmont had 10 of its 11 players score points. Worley reflected on Piedmont’s lock-down defense in the second half. “I thought our defense and our communication was great. I think we have the ability to have any player guard anyone at any position,” said Worley. It was an impressive performance by sophomore guard and first-year varsity starter Raji Silverberg, who scored 10 points with five assists and five steals. “It’s his first time playing point guard. We’re expecting good things from him but also hope he can limit those mistakes that typically come from younger players like sophomores. I think he’s going to be a great player coming up, he’s strong defensively and gets in the passing lanes,” said Worley. Final scorers include: Harris with 26 points and 10 boards. Burden had 19 points and nine rebounds. Theo Evans made a 3-pointer, while Matthew Riordan, Alex Anderson, Teagan Haddawy, Arjun Bornstein, Matteo Costa, and Declan Linnane had two points. It opens against Richmond on Thursday at 8:30 p.m. Northgate, which were last year’s NCS Open Division semifinalists. Windsor will play Hamilton HS from Los Angeles. Acalanes takes on Archie Williams, which also competes in Division 3 against Piedmont and made last year’s semifinals.

articles.text: Staff Photo Skylar Best placed 64th place at the State meet and was the 11th fastest freshman in the state. Piedmont High freshman Skylar Best was the lone qualifier from the cross-country team to qualify for the CIF State Championship on Saturday, November 26, at Woodward Park in Fresno. She finished 64th out of 201 runners with a time of 19:56.2, and was the 11th fastest freshman in the state. “I’m really proud to even make it there as a freshman. The competition was really tough but that inspires me to improve and train hard to get back there next year. It definitely meant a lot to me personally to race there. The environment was amazing and I just had a great time,” said Best. Piedmont has now sent at least one runner to the prestigious event for 34 consecutive years. It was just Best’s second time competing on a 5K course, eclipsing her previous best of 22:14.1 at a league meet at Oyster Bay in San Leandro on October 19. “This was a 5K instead of a three-mile that we usually raced this season,” explained Best. “It felt like a great end to the season. I had a really fast first mile and wanted to try and stay in the front area of the pack. The course had a lot of rolling hills and two steep hills.” they were freshmen, including Sophia Zalewski (2016, 20:06.3) and Ellie Black, (2018, 20:37.7). Piedmont’s varsity team should have a large slate of returners in 2023 after featuring junior Jamie Schwarz, sophomores Ella Yasar and Caroline Taylor, and some standout freshmen like Cora Chun, Elia Kwong, Quincy Antaya, Amina Green, and, of course, Best. Her time at Woodward Park was better than several previous star runners from Piedmont when Skylar Best, the only Piedmont cross-country runner to qualify for the State meet, was consistently the lead runner for the girls’ team throughout the season. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team began its season with a 3-2 loss to Miramonte at Witter Field on Monday, November 28. The Highlanders were still without several players with the club soccer season not over. “We were still missing a few players but that’s usually the case at this time of the season with players finishing the club season and doing showcases,” said coach Dan Chubbock. Still the Highlanders played well against the Matadors and held the lead twice before halftime when the score was tied at 2-2. Miramonte scored the eventual game-winner around 10 minutes into the second half. The Matadors, notably, competes in Division 3 of North Coast Section while Piedmont plays one division below them. “We actually played well in the second half but they managed to get the goal and we just couldn’t quite find the finishing touch,” said Chubbock. Piedmont’s Michaela Bini, who also is a member of the tennis team, struck first for the Highlanders just a few minutes into the start of the game on an assist from freshman Miranda Liu. Later on in the first half, Liu scored the first goal of her high school career on a long ball over the defenders from Charlotte Davies. articles.text: The 2022 World Cup is shaping up with its usual upsets and Cinderella tales. The Group stage wraps up this week with Groups A and B officially settled. The U.S. fought down to the wire against Iran to overtake them 1-0 on Tuesday to send the Stars and Stripes onto the Round of 16. After posting ties in its first two games, it marked the team’s first win. It tied Wales 1-1 in the Cup opener on November 21, and then did well to hold tournament favorite England to a scoreless draw last Friday. Here’s a recap of how the World Cup is shaping up. Group B: No. 5 England (7 points, clinched), No. 16 USA (5 points, clinched), No. 20 Iran (3 points), No. 19 Wales (1 point) The Americans got the job done. The stress from watching may have taken some years off of our lives, but they are through to the Round of 16. Christian Pulisic scored the only goal – arguably the most important goal of his U.S. career º in the 38th minute against Iran, but had to leave the game at halftime after suffering an abdominal injury The U.S. sat deeper in the latter 45 minutes but did well to not concede any goals. They allowed just one shot on target throughout the night. Iran argued for a penalty in the waning minutes of second-half stoppage time, but the ref ruled Iranian forward Mehdi Taremi went down too easily (called a flop). Looking ahead, the Americans are now set to face No. 8 ranked Netherlands. The two sides have played five times, with the Dutchmen dominating the series at 4-0- 1. They. haven’t faced each other since June 2015, where Holland won a friendly 4-3. The Netherlands will be tough with one of the more balanced rosters in the tournament, led by a stout defense with Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk and Bayern’s Matthijs de Ligt. For what it’s worth, I picked the Dutch making the Quarterfinals, but I also had the U.S. not getting out of the group. Group A: No. 8 Netherlands (7 points, clinched), No. 18 Senegal (6 points, clinched), No. 44 Ecuador (4 points), No. 50 Qatar (0 points) The Dutch opened with a 2-0 win over Senegal, tied 1-1 with Ecuador, and beat Qatar 2-0 to solidify the top spot. Senegal, meanwhile, overtook Ecuador on Tuesday for the second spot with a big 2-1 win. It marks the first time the Senegalese reach the Round of 16 since 2002 when they made the quarterfinals. Netherlands faces the U.S. on December 3 at 6:00 a.m., while Senegal will be the underdogs against England the following day at 11:00 a.m. Group C: No. 26 Poland (4 points), No. 3 Argentina (3 points), No. 51 Saudi Arabia (3 points), No. 13 Mexico (1 points) Today’s Group C matches have both qualification spots up for grabs with Poland facing Argentina and Saudi Arabia squaring off with Mexico. Argentina managed to keep itself in the race and avoided a meltdown with a 2-nil win over Mexico. Right now, Poland holds the top spot by one point and one-goal in differential. Although El Tri of Mexico sits Photo courtesy of ABC13 The U.S. Men’s cocker team is through to the next round thanks to Christian Pulisic’s goal in a 1-0 win over Iran. in last with a single point, they are technically not dead in the water just yet. Poland holds 1C with a win over Argentina or with a tie if Saudi Arabia loses to Mexico. Poland would be out of the tournament with a loss and Saudi Arabia win. Argentina guarantees a spot by defeating Poland and wins the group with a loss or tie from Saudi Arabia. If the Arabian Falcons and Argentina wins and are tied at six points each, the tiebreaker would be goal differential—which Argentina leads by two goals. Should the two become tied in goal differential, the tiebreaker becomes goals scored and then head-to-head if the goal tally is also tied. Mexico must beat Saudi Arabia to give itself a chance and a win by four or more goals guarantees a spot. If Mexico wins and Argentina loses, El Tri finishes second. If Argentina ties against Poland, Mexico would need to win by three goals to qualify. If Mexico wins by four or more goals, they would finish second. take 2E with a win and Japan losing to Spain. If Japan ties, Germany needs a multi-goal win to finish ahead of Japan on goal differential. Group F: No. 12 Croatia (4 points), No. 22 Morocco (4 points), No. 2 Belgium (3 points), No. 41 Canada (0 points) Group F also plays on Thursday with Croatia, Morocco and Belgium in contention, and in that order. The Moroccans stunned top-ranked Belgium 2-0 on Sunday, November 27, while Croatia knocked out Canada from contention 4-1 that same day. Belgium, which I had making the semifinals, is looking like their life is in doubt against a tough Croatian side, with Morocco just needing to get the job done versus Canada. A tie won’t be enough for Belgium to make it out of the group, but they can win the group with a win and a Morocco loss or tie. Group D: No. 4 France (6 points, clinched), No. 38 Australia (3 points), No. 10 Denmark (1 point), No. 35 Tunisia (1 point) France is perhaps in the best form of the tournament at 2-0 with a 4-1 win over Australia to open and a strong 2-1 defeat of Denmark. PSG star Kylian Mbappe is a real difference maker, once again, with three goals—two of which coming against the Danes. Already clinched France is set to close the tournament today against Tunisia and is looking like a clear favorite for the Coupe du Monde. Today, Denmark could fight its way to the Round of 16 by defeating Australia, where the Socceroos just require a tie to qualify. Group E: No. 7 Spain (4 points), No. 24 Japan (3 points), No. 31 Costa Rica (3 points), No. 11 Germany (1 points) Thursday’s slate of Group E games include Spain taking on Japan and Germany versus Costa Rica, with each qualification spot available for all four teams. Spain can qualify by tying Japan and can earn 1E with win, or a tie would still earn the top spot with a Costa Rica loss or draw to Germany. Japan can win the group by defeating Spain and will automatically qualify regardless of Costa Rica’s results based on goal differential, where the Japanese holds a six-goal advantage. Germany is on the verge of being knocked out in the group stage for the second consecutive World Cup, but they can still fight from death with a victory against Costa Rica at the bare minimum. The Germans Group G: No. 1 Brazil (6 points, clinched), No. 15 Switzerland (3 points), No. 43 Cameroon (1 point), No. 21 Serbia (1 point) Brazil was the first team to clinch a spot into the next round after beating Switzerland 1-0 on Monday. The second qualification spot will likely come down to Switzerland against Serbia on Friday at 11:00 a.m. with Cameroon taking on the Canaries of Brazil. A tie won’t do it for Serbia, who I had as a potential that that could surprise its way to the quarterfinals. Serbia must win to overtake Switzerland for the second spot, they’ll need a peak performance from Fulham striker Aleksandar Mitrović and require Juventus forward Dusan Vlahović to quickly recover from his injury. Group H: No. 9 Portugal (6 points, clinched), No. 61 Ghana (3 points), No. 28 South Korea (1 point), No. 14 Uruguay (1 point) Portugal has already clinched its spot to the next round and will face South Korea, which needs a win to stay alive, on Friday at 7:00 a.m. The second spot is still up for grabs with Ghana and Uruguay competing at 11:00 a.m., and things can certainly get messy. If Ghana wins, they are in. If they draw and South Korea draws or loses, they finish second. If Ghana draws and South Korea wins by one goal, the two sides will be equal on goal differential and the winner will be determined by goals scored— which Ghana currently leads 5-2. If South Korea wins by two or more goals, South Korea will move to second. If Uruguay wins, they finish second if South Korea draws or loses. Uruguay will be the favorite against Ghana, but have been another disappointment after walking in as the favorite to earn 2H.

Group A: No. 8 Netherlands (7 points, clinched), No. 18 Senegal (6 points, clinched), No. 44 Ecuador (4 points), No. 50 Qatar (0 points) The Dutch opened with a 2-0 win over Senegal, tied 1-1 with Ecuador, and beat Qatar 2-0 to solidify the top spot. Senegal, meanwhile, overtook Ecuador on Tuesday for the second spot with a big 2-1 win. It marks the first time the Senegalese reach the Round of 16 since 2002 when they made the quarterfinals. Netherlands faces the U.S. on December 3 at 6:00 a.m., while Senegal will be the underdogs against England the following day at 11:00 a.m. Group C: No. 26 Poland (4 points), No. 3 Argentina (3 points), No. 51 Saudi Arabia (3 points), No. 13 Mexico (1 points) Today’s Group C matches have both qualification spots up for grabs with Poland facing Argentina and Saudi Arabia squaring off with Mexico. Poland holds 1C with a win over Argentina or with a tie if Saudi Arabia loses to Mexico. Poland would be out of the tournament with a loss and Saudi Arabia win. Argentina guarantees a spot by defeating Poland and wins the group with a loss or tie from Saudi Arabia. If the Arabian Falcons and Argentina wins and are tied at six points each, the tiebreaker would be goal differential—which Argentina leads by two goals. Should the two become tied in goal differential, the tiebreaker becomes goals scored and then head-to-head if the goal tally is also tied. Mexico must beat Saudi Arabia to give itself a chance and a win by four or more goals guarantees a spot. If Mexico wins and Argentina loses, El Tri finishes second. Japan can win the group by defeating Spain and will automatically qualify regardless of Costa Rica’s results based on goal differential, where the Japanese holds a six-goal advantage. articles.text: Photo by Drew Altizer Hung Liu speaks at the opening of a retrospective art exhibit honoring her work. De Young Museum celebrates the legacy of Hung Liu with Golden Gate, an exhibition displayed in the museum’s Wilsey Court through January 8. Liu was one of the most important Chinese-born artists working in the United States, and specifically in Oakland. This installation reimagines some of her most iconic paintings through her own personal history as a Chinese-born artist, placing herself among the migrants who arrived in California by both land and sea. The artist died suddenly in August 2021, prompting the museum to extend the exhibition’s closing date to 2023. “Hung Liu was such a vibrant and vital part of the art world in the Bay Area and beyond,” said museum curator Jana Keegan. “Her art practice focused on recovering the stories of people who have been often forgotten in traditional historical narratives. The legacy and wonderful oeuvre she leaves behind will ensure that she too will always be remembered.” Liu tells the story of migration and displacement throughout the United States in her artwork. One of her most iconic paintings, Resident Alien, is the focal point of the exhibition. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/ hung-liu.

articles.text: Brass concert, Holiday Blast, this Sunday at 4 p.m. Berkeley Symphony will ring in this holiday season with Holiday Blast, where the Berkeley Symphony Brass Quintet will perform festive favorites at Piedmont Community Hall on Sunday, December 4, at 4 p.m. Holiday Blast is part of the chamber music series in Piedmont and will feature pieces from J.S. Bach to Duke Ellington. Guests are invited to join a free outdoor reception following the concert, where they can enjoy sweet and savory treats and libations, including hot seasonal beverages. Tickets are $35 and are available online at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800. The concert celebrates the 10th anniversary of its Chamber Series, and will honor Gray Cathrall, a founding board member of the Piedmont Center for the Arts and editor of the Piedmont Post. Cathrall has been integral to the partnership between Berkeley Symphony. “Ten years ago, Gray came to us with a bold idea to produce a Berkeley Symphony chamber music series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts,” said René Mandel, Artistic Director of Berkeley Symphony. “We are grateful to our eclectic, enthusiastic, and devoted audiences at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. We marvel at the wonderful works of art that grace its walls and enhance our performances. We are profoundly grateful to Gray for his unwavering support and service to this jewel of a series and to the entire East Bay community.” Performing music will be the Berkeley Symphony Brass Quintet, John Pearson (Trumpet), Scott Macomber (Trumpet), Meredith Brown (Horn), Tom Hornig (Tenor Trombone), and Peter Wahrhaftig (Tuba). The big brass sound of the quintet will play a lively program that features J.S. Bach’s “My Spirit Be Joyful,” Music from the Royal Fireworks by G.F. Handel, Morley Calvert’s Suite from “Monteregian Hills,” a selection by Duke Ellington, including “Cottontail Capers,” “Sophisticated Lady,” “It Don’t Mean a Thing if it Ain’t Got That Swing,” and “Boy Meets Horn.”

articles.text: Orchestra to perform Duke Ellington’s Nutcracker Suite The Marcus Shelby Orchestra will perform Duke Ellington’s Nutcracker Suite at SF Jazz this Friday, December 2. A bass player, composer, and arranger, Shelby modeled his Orchestra after Duke Ellington’s and cites the jazz luminary as an inspiration for him musically. He has served as Artist in Residence at Yerba Buena Gardens Festival in San Francisco and Composer in Residence at Intersection for Arts. He Marcus Shelby was appointed to the San Francisco Arts Commission in 2013. He and his orchestra are regular performers at San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz. Local artist Michael Stehr will open his newest exhibition, entitled “Lost in the Shadows,” at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, December 3, at 11:30 a.m. The exhibit includes 42 new paintings, and 80 total works of art, and will be on display through December 18. Stehr will use some of his new paintings to explore the power of shadow in painting. While it is light that often contributes animation and luminosity to a composition, it is the absence of this light, shadow, that makes the presence of that light much more tangible. Without light, there cannot be shadow. But without shadow, the effect of light is greatly mitigated. Indeed, the two must work hand in hand, for it is the contrasts between bright and dark values, light and shadow, that do much to provide visual interest to a painting. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays December 3-4, 10-11, and 17-18. Masks and proof of vaccination are required at the Center.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite, Nutcracker, premieres on Thursday, December 8, at the War Memorial Opera House. The ballet will be performed through December 27. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s 90-year history. San Francisco Ballet performs the production every year, with a kaleidoscope of 150 dancers telling the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco. San Francisco Symphony will perform the familiar score of Tchaikovsky. A diverse array of instruments are used by the Symphony, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani – all played by only three musicians. Scenic design is by Michael Yeargan; costume design is by Martin Pakledinaz; lighting design is by James F. Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall K. Harrington. The ballet is especially appropriate for children aged five and older. No children under age three will be permitted. The performance Nutcracker runs two hours with one intermission. Tickets are selling quickly for performances on Christmas Eve, December 24. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker-dec-2022/. articles.text: Turkey… The very word conjures up a multitude of images. It could be fun activities like the Turkey Trot in Piedmont on Thanksgiving morning. At the opposite end of the spectrum, it is insulting to be called a turkey. But the bird itself is certainly beautiful and conjures up some beautiful thoughts. Some people even consider that its beauty should make it the national bird of America. You may remember that the turkey was the origin of a great national debate. When our Founding Fathers were discussing what bird should be the national symbol, John Adams wanted it to be the eagle. Thomas Jefferson wanted the dove. Benjamin Franklin proposed the turkey and gave many good reasons. The eagle won. However, the turkey is a much more important bird. Please read on. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s production of Guiseppe Verdi’s masterpiece La Traviata ends this Sunday, December 3. Tickets are still available for the closing performance. Music Director Eun Sun Kim leads the Opera Orchestra and chorus in Shawna Lucey’s production of the three-act production. South African-born Pretty Yende sings the lead role as Violetta Valéry. Yende has appeared in the same role in the Vienna State Opera, Naples’ Teatro di San Carlo, Royal Opera, Paris Opera productions. Jonathan Tetelman is cast in the lead male role as Alfredo Germont, a young bourgeois from a provincial family who admires Violetta from afar. “Verdi’s masterpiece about one of the most incredible women in history lives at the intersection of sex and money,” said Director Shawna Lucey. “Marie Duplessis, or Violetta as she is known in the opera, through her own ingenuity and tenacity has become Paris’ most famous courtesan.” The opera is set to an Italian libretto by Francesco Piave and is based on the famous play by Alexandre Dumas. The opera us three hours with two intermissions. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfopera.com/operas/ la-traviata/. There are as many recipes for turkey a la king as there were for King Louis of France. Here is an easy one: this will serve two diners. To serve four, just double the recipe. Dice half an onion and one clove of garlic and put into a sauté pan to caramelize along with a little oil, a little salt and white pepper. Finally chop some celery and add it to the pan. Add a handful of chopped mushrooms and continue to cook. Cover this with about 8 ounces of your turkey soup and 2 tablespoons of sour cream and about 4 tablespoons of cream sherry. Take two handfuls of chopped leftover turkey and put in the pan and just warm it. You can even add some peas if you like. This mixture can be served with polenta, rice or on top of toast. You can use this exact same recipe to make a turkey pot pie. All you have to do is line an oven-proof dish with polenta, add your turkey mixture, and then top with the remaining polenta. Bake in the oven at 425° for about 40 minutes. Nothing could be easier or more beautiful. articles.text: For those of you who are part of that solid sci-fi fan base and who especially enjoy what I think of as space container films, you will not be disappointed with Life. It borrows heavily from the iconic Ridley Scott film, Alien (a movie that likely will never be its equal. I would judge Life as a film at top of a list of B-movies, rich in production value with top tier actors, resulting in an engaging if predictable story. In brief, a crew of six astronauts is just completing an eightmonth trip to Mars where they have collected soil samples to be returned to the NASA labs back on earth. For now, they are spending their days on the International Space Station waiting for a ride home. First an introduction of the crew: Dr. David Jordan (Jake Gyllenhaal), team doc and pilot; Rory Adams (Ryan Reynolds), the crew’s MacGyver; Miranda North (Rebecca Ferguson), CDC rep and quarantine expert; Hugh Derry (Ariyon Bakare), botanist; and Sho Kendo (Hiroyuki Sanada), backup everyman. No surprise, botanist Hugh is fascinated with examining the soil samples, probing for any signs of life. And, unexpectedly, as he adds oxygen, liquid, and stimulation to a sample he discovers a single-cell amoeba-like organism that moves and seems to benignly react to his examination. Hiroyuki Sanada in a scene from the movie Life. Veterans of Sci-fi films know that when a crew is confined on a ship floating in space in a hostile environment, it’s best to leave well enough alone. Seal the room and wait. But Hugh is far too curious and the idea of finding life on Mars is compelling, bordering on the miraculous. So, he repeatedly returns to the organism, which is mutating in small ways. Meanwhile the rest of the crew is relaxed, hanging out, running through the usual check-all-systems drills, and, with the exception of Jordan, all eager to get home. But keep in mind that movies of this type are not written to give the audience much character backstory. The purpose is to create a crisis and turn those aboard loose as they struggle to control their panic while desperately searching for an existential solution. It’s always high stakes. And naturally – just wait for it – there is a crisis, one that puts all six astronauts in harm’s way. I’ll say no more about the plot. But to the film’s credit it manages to create a solid dread factor, meaning that this is not likely to end well. Hollywood is superb at creating this motif (think The Panic Room with Jodie Foster as example). Space ship/horror movies are the perfect milieu for such tension-filled stories. What happens in Life, well you can imagine. Or not. What you can’t anticipate is the ending. It has a nice nihilistic twist and is completely unexpected. Life. Directed by Daniel Epinosa. Starring Jake Gyllenhaal, Rebecca Ferguson, Ryan Reynolds. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated R. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Frederich Nietzche once wrote, “…if you gaze long enough into the abyss, the abyss will gaze into you.” As is profoundly depicted in the film 12 Years a Slave, released in 2013. Slavery, in all its malignant cruelty, is that abyss. The institution of slavery was an embedded pathology that gripped our nation for more than a century, initially made manifest in the plantations of the South and buttressed by the virulent prejudice and discrimination that rippled through antebellum and post-antebellum America. The word “holocaust” has been reserved to depict the atrocities of the concentration camps of Germany during World War II, crafted from the darkest parts of the human heart. Slavery is viewed through a different prism, though it too is a nightmare that was abhorrent in the extreme, with human beings reduced to mere chattel. When viewed across history it also seems incomprehensible. 12 Years a Slave is a powerful and unyielding view of one man’s journey into the heart of the South in the year 1841. His name was Solomon Northrup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a freeman, prosperous, and living in Saratoga, N.Y., with his wife and two children. Kidnapped, he awakens one morning in a dark room, in chains, and soon finds himself sold and resold, ending up on a Louisiana plantation. His master, Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender), is a ruthless and sadistic slave owner, so unhinged that he is blind to his own depravity, and the depravity of his wife (Sarah Paulson), who urges him to shred the backs of the less productive slaves while knowing that her husband rapes the young women. Solomon soon understands that he has descended into one of the circles of hell and he bears witness to the personal torment of the slaves with whom he shares his existence. It is an existence that is, in every respect, filled with an acute and daily privation that seems unendurable. He faces his new life in the context of the life from which he was snatched. He was a musician, educated, with a family that filled his world and now floods his memories. The power of 12 Years a Slave resides in its unremitting honesty. There are no benevolent owners, not even Master Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch), who, while humane, still views his slaves as forced free labor and not as people. In one wrenching scene he buys a young black woman at auction, but not her two children. In another harrowing scene, Solomon is hung by the neck by an overseer, his toes barely touching the ground, and though Ford eventually cuts him down, he is incapable of viewing that moment for what it is: heinous and monstrous. Like all those involved in slavery, Epps and Ford were incapable of viewing the pain it exacted, or seeing it as an evil of such magnitude that it shriveled the souls of those who perpetuated it and it laid ruin to those who lost more than their freedom. That is what 12 Years a Slave conveys, absent stereotypes and unnecessary melodrama. This film is a spare narrative, based on the story written by Solomon Northrup, a memoir that has stood the test of time and finally has found its way, remarkably, to the screen. 12 Years a Slave. Directed by Steve McQueen. Starring Chiwetel Ejiofor, Michael Fassbender, Benedict Cumberbatch. 2 hrs,, 14 min. Rated R. Released in 2013, Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ HBO MAX.

articles.text: The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society I realize is a mouthful as titles go, but it is a film worth finding, charming and an old-fashioned drama with a superb ensemble cast, led by Lily James as Juliet Ashton and Michael Huisman portraying Dawsey Adams. Based on the best-selling novel by Mary Shafer and Annie Barrows, the story opens in London in 1946, and World War II has just ended. Reminders of the damage to the city by German blitzes are seen on street after street; many buildings are mere scorched shells. Yet the Brits are determined to carry on, and much relieved that they have prevailed. Juliet, a novelist who lost her parents in a bombing raid, has just published a book titled Izzy Bickerstaff Goes to War. With the encouragement of her editor, Sidney Stark (Matthew Goode), she is giving readings at small bookshops. After one such appearance she is asked by Sidney to write an essay for the London Times about the importance of reading. It captures her interest, however she wonders where to begin. Simultaneously she receives a letter from Dawsey, a farmer living on Guernsey Island. He asks her if she might be able to find a particular book for him. Though the island is located closer to France than England, and was part of the English Crown, it was occupied by the German forces. Dawsey explains in the letter that during the war he was part of a book club with a strange long name, a group of six or seven people that continued even after the Germans had left. Intrigued, Juliet thinks of her essay assignment and this unusual literary society and convinces Sidney that she should visit the island and interview the club members, focusing on how reading got them through the occupation. As it turns out, just before boarding a ship for the journey, she accepts a marriage proposal by an American officer, Mark Reynolds, who places a stunning ring on her finger. Arriving on Guernsey, she is impressed with its extraordinary vistas. She manages to find the local postmaster, Eden Ramsey (Tom Courtenay), who is the titular head of the society, and is invited to a society gathering where she is asked to give a reading. On a dark evening she meets the members and through a 1941 flashback learns how the eccentric name came about. She assumed her visit to the island would be brief; however, she soon learns that there is a tragic tale needing to be told, a mystery of sorts, and so she extends her time on Guernsey, growing ever fonder of the people, especially farmer Dawsey, though ever reminded of her engagement to Mark. Guernsey is more than engaging as a film. It is both touching, superbly acted, and a perfect period tale, enjoyable to its most satisfying conclusion. The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society. Directed by Mike Newell. Starring Lily James, Matthew Goode, and Michael Huisman. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Now streaming on Netflix. Lily James and Michiel Huisman in a scene from The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society.

articles.text: The children’s classic Black Beauty was written by Anna Swell in 1887 and has managed to endure for well over a century, told and retold in books and on the screen. Note that the film I’m recommending in this review was released by Disney+ in 2020, and represents a complete overhaul of the story. Where the original narrative by Sewell is set in Dickensian Victorian England, and Black Beauty is a male mustang (voiced in the 1994 film by Alan Cummings), this most recent release flips the gender of Black Beauty who is now voiced by Kate Winslet. The story begins in the American West where the young colt (not yet named) roams free with her mother in the Onaqui Mountains of Utah. Free that is until some cowboys round up the wild horses, and in the process separate the youngster from her mother; the two never to be reunited. As it turns out, the young mustang catches the attention of horse trainer John Manley (Iain Glen) who takes her to a horse sanctuary named Birtwick. Though the horse likes Manley, it is nevertheless rebellious and uncooperative, trying the patience of the trainer. At the same time, Manley Mackenzie Foy stars in the Disney remake of Black Beauty. receives the tragic news that his sister and her husband have been killed in a traffic accident and he is asked to care for his young niece, Jo Green (Mackenzie Foy), a teenager. Though Jo makes it clear to her uncle that she is unhappy with the situation, and still grieving, the black mustang catches her attention, and wisely Manley puts the difficult horse in the care of Jo, asking her also to work in the stables. As it turns out, the horse (which Jo names Black Beauty) and the teen become close, recognizing that each has suffered a loss. And so begins act two of the movie. To Jo’s distress, Manley tells her that because Birtwick is in need of money, Black Beauty may have to be sold. Jo makes a deal with the owner of the sanctuary that she will work extra hours and earn enough money to buy Black Beauty. Nevertheless, the horse is sold, and the setting of the film shifts dramatically from Utah to England. The story evolves as Jo searches for Black Beauty. The horse ends up being sold several times, first to an upper class English family, to a farmer, then to a New York carriage driver. Meanwhile the Beauty and Jo yearn to be reunited and the search continues. Black Beauty. Directed by Ashley Avis. Starring Kate Winslet, Mackenzie Foy, Iain Glen. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG. Released 2020. Now Streaming on Disney+, Mackenzie Foy and Iain Glen in a scene from Black Beauty.

articles.text: A scene from Ice Age: Continental Drift. Ice Age: Continental Drift is the fourth installment of what has proved to be a kid friendly (7-8 years-old) franchise, with the familiar characters – Manny the wooly mammoth (Ray Romano), Sid the sloth (John Leguizamo), and Diego the saber-toothed tiger (Denis Leary) – who return for another adventure. Added to this cohort is a new character, Sid’s sassy granny (Wanda Sykes). Of course they encounter natural disasters, predators, engage in wacky antics, and naturally learn life lessons that revolve around friendship and family. There are avalanches, tidal waves, and even a tornado for added excitement. But perhaps the best four minutes of this animated feature belong to the now favorite prehistoric, bug-eyed squirrel called Scrat (Chris Wedge), ever in the hunt for that elusive acorn. He never utters a word; instead, he makes squeaky noises as he remains in hot pursuit of that nut that is always not quite within his grasp. Scrat is a truly inspired character. In this story, the trio and granny navigate the open waters, trapped on a large chunk if ice. articles.text: It may seem like a lifetime ago when you gazed down at your first grandchild with your eyes tearing up and your heart full of love. Just like the new parents, you looked at the beauty of that innocent little bundle and unconsciously began thinking about the years ahead; how the child would grow, learn, play, make friends, become an active part of your family and a positive member of the community that they live in. Now fast forward five, ten, 15 years. Things have changed and not for the better. You have a troubled grandchild. Maybe your grandchild’s problems began in pre-school when the parents were repeatedly being contacted by the teachers about the behavior of hitting or not following directions. Maybe your grandchild has been identified as being a mean kid in elementary school by the teachers or the principal who feel that they are a ringleader who coerces others into negative behavior in the classroom and after school. Or perhaps you have a grandteen who has been in trouble with the law for drug use, underage drinking, or other anti-social behaviors that have led them into formal interactions with the criminal justice system. There are an infinite number of factors that contribute to children having the kinds of struggles described here, and therefore, just as many ways to approach solutions. Some parents try to cope with their children’s behavior problems with severe consequences or punishment – the Tough Love approach. Others simply bury their heads or throw up their hands, not knowing exactly what to do and fearing making things worse. What’s wrong with the Tough Love approach? One may argue that anything else is coddling, ignoring, and enabling the child’s negative/destructive/dangerous behaviors, and that things will simply get worse and worse by not applying strict boundaries and punishments. Although it’s possible that in expert hands, short-term success can result when troubled kids and teens see that their behaviors have consequences, and that the adults in their lives will hold them to a specific set of behaviors or else they will be punished. Children can be troubled and have dark feelings. As a grandparent, you can help them. In the long run however, this approach may result in breaking the young person’s sense of trust in those who are supposed to love and understand them. The young person may end up having fractured relationships with the very adults who tried to address the issues in this way. Another way to view the troubled child or teen is to try to look beyond their behavior to what is underlying the child’s actions. Most people, children included, are behaving in ways that they believe are advantageous to them in some way, even when it seems paradoxical to the observer. The pressures on young people today are enormous and very different from stresses that the older generation experienced. The possible causes are endless, and it may be that professional help is needed to find the underlying motivation. What’s a grandparent to do? Grandparents play a special role in children’s lives. Unlike the parents, grandparents enjoy a few degrees of separation in a child’s life and can usually be absolved of the disciplinary role in the troubled child’s world. (Grandparents raising grandchildren as primary custodians are the exception, of course). Instead, a grandparent can be the source of unconditional love, compassion, and understanding. Ask your grandchild to share their feelings with you confidentially. Remind them that you love them no matter what and that you will always be there for them. Pose questions such as: • “How has this (insert situation, experience, dilemma) been for you?” • “What were you feeling when that was happening?” • “What might make things easier for you?” • “How can I be part of making things better for you?” • “What if you had a magic wand? What one thing would you wish for?” Many adults who have recovered from severe difficulties in their childhood/teens/young adulthood, such as addiction, abusive relationships, gang membership, criminal activity, and/or incarceration, will point to one person in their life who always believed in them and always made them feel loved and understood. More often than not it’s a grandparent, a person who had the vision to see beyond the behavior to the person inside. It may take years for a person to recognize how that love made the difference for them in their life, but it can and does happen. Be that special person in your troubled grandchild’s life. Children can be troubled and have dark feelings. As a grandparent, you can help them. In the long run however, this approach may result in breaking the young person’s sense of trust in those who are supposed to love and understand them. The young person may end up having fractured relationships with the very adults who tried to address the issues in this way. Another way to view the troubled child or teen is to try to look beyond their behavior to what is underlying the child’s actions. Most people, children included, are behaving in ways that they believe are advantageous to them in some way, even when it seems paradoxical to the observer. The pressures on young people today are enormous and very different from stresses that the older generation experienced. The possible causes are endless, and it may be that professional help is needed to find the underlying motivation. What’s a grandparent to do? Grandparents play a special role in children’s lives. Unlike the parents, grandparents enjoy a few degrees of separation in a child’s life and can usually be absolved of the disciplinary role in the troubled child’s world. (Grandparents raising grandchildren as primary custodians are the exception, of course). Instead, a grandparent can be the source of unconditional love, compassion, and understanding. Ask your grandchild to share their feelings with you confidentially. Remind them that you love them no matter what and that you will always be there for them. Pose questions such as: • “How has this (insert situation, experience, dilemma) been for you?” • “What were you feeling when that was happening?” • “What might make things easier for you?” • “How can I be part of making things better for you?” • “What if you had a magic wand? What one thing would you wish for?” Many adults who have recovered from severe difficulties in their childhood/teens/young adulthood, such as addiction, abusive relationships, gang membership, criminal activity, and/or incarceration, will point to one person in their life who always believed in them and always made them feel loved and understood. More often than not it’s a grandparent, a person who had the vision to see beyond the behavior to the person inside. It may take years for a person to recognize how that love made the difference for them in their life, but it can and does happen. Be that special person in your troubled grandchild’s life. Dear Macmama: I see there is an update to a new operating system, Ventura, OS 13. I currently have Big Sur OS12.6. Is there any reason to update, any new features? -Geoff, Piedmont Dear Geoff: Each new operating system comes with new features, sometimes responding to customers’ feedback, and Ventura is no different. Most likely, if the applications that you use are working fine with Big Sur, they should work well with Ventura. There are cases of applications that are not Ventura-ready, so it would be important for you to look up the compatibility of the applications that you use the most. But yes, there are some exciting features that many customers have been requesting for a long time. Here are just a few. 1. Get rid of duplicate photos: This is a feature that customers and tech pros I like have been asking to have available for years. It’s finally here. In your Photos app, if there are duplicates available, there will be a “Duplicates”, listed in the sidebar. You can then select the ones you want to merge. This will not remove any photos from your albums, and merge all the copies you may have, and put the extras in “Recently Deleted” in Photos. When I ran this utility, I was able to get rid of almost 2000 photos. 2. Schedule when to send an email, and undo send: Scheduling an email to be sent or undoing a sent email was something we used to have to use a thirdparty app for, but now through the Mail app, these are both possible. You have up to 10 seconds to “unsend” an email message, and you can also select a date and time to remind you to get back to a message that you want to read later in your inbox. 3. Use your iPhone as a webcam: The camera on your laptop is OK, but the camera on your iPhone is much better. As a matter of fact, it’s much better than many of the Webcams that are out there. This function is called “Continuity Camera”. To enable this, you simply bring your iPhone near your Mac, making sure they are both on the same Wi-Fi network, or that Bluetooth is enabled, and your iPhone will appear as an available WebCam in FaceTime, Zoom and other video communication apps. Apple sells a MagSafe stand for laptops for $30 made by Belkin that allows you to clip the stand with your phone magnetically attached to the top of your screen. They will be making one for monitors and desktop computers soon. 4. Enhanced Spotl ight Search: It seems that with every operating system upgrade the search function gets better. This is definitely the case in Ventura. Spotlight now allows you to open an QuickLook item with Preview. To do this, you select the item in the list of search results and press your spacebar. More excitingly, though, spotlight allows you to search for photos by searching their location and by searching their type. For example, you can search “dog” and your dog photos will come up. In my experience this function is pretty good but will definitely need to be improved. There are many features in Ventura, like “undo send” in Messages, Hand-off in FaceTime (switch from your phone to your Mac seamlessly while on a FaceTime call), and a completely refreshed System Settings (previously System Preferences). These features, and some new features to come in further updates, make Ventura a worthy update to the line of operating systems from Apple. Those who want to drive the opposite way have to patiently wait for several minutes until the road is clear to proceed. The views are certainly worth the wait. It is a favorite spot for surfers and beachcombers alike. The views of the Golden Gate Bridge and surrounding areas are breathtaking, and the scenery alone merits a visit. The next stop was at the Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito. It had been closed to the public due to COVID. The Seniors felt privileged to be allowed inside as the Mammal Center has only recently opened their doors and are very strict. For example, one must show evidence of COVID vaccinations, show identification, and wear facial coverings. The animals need to be protected as well as people. Founded as a non-profit in 1975, It is home to the world’s largest marine mammal hospital, which provides life-saving care to animals so they can be safely released back to the ocean. It has been acknowledged that marine mammal health, ocean health, and human health are linked. The work of the Center advances medical knowledge and understanding about these links to inspire consumers to try to change their behavior to protect our future. When you visit, sign up for the docent tours; they make all the difference in understanding the work done by the Center. The Seniors saw sea lions, elephant seals, and other sea life needing rescuing. The docents spoke about sustainable seafood and conservation. One can even symbolically adopt a released patient through their “Adopt a-Seal” program and give the next sick animal a second chance at life. It is a great place to take families and groups of all ages, and it is handicapped accessible. They even have a separate dining room with floor to ceiling windows which would make a perfect setting for a special occasion. Lunch wouldn’t be complete without a stop at Lappert’s ice cream shop across from the restaurant. Though the shop is small in size, the ice cream is hard to beat. articles.text: Did you know that gratitude can make you a better caregiver? Being thankful can help reduce anxiety and allow us to cope better with stress. It can also boost optimism, improve focus, increase happiness and improve sleep. The holidays provide the perfect opportunity to count your blessings and practice being grateful. As a caregiver, you may have your fair share of frustrating and exhausting days. However, even in the hard moments, there are many reasons to be thankful for the opportunity to help others. Here are four reasons to be grateful this holiday season for your caregiving experience: 1. Your work is meaningful At the beginning of every morning, you can wake up knowing that you will truly make a difference in someone’s life that day. You may feel like your day is filled with repetitive tasks like helping to cook meals or clean the house. However, all those little things you do result in a huge impact on the lives of those you serve. Without you, they would struggle with physical and emotional challenges and would not be able to live life to the fullest. Since you chose to be a caregiver, you have the power to transform someone’s day, week, and ultimately, their life. 2. Lessons from work can enrich your personal life As a caregiver, you develop many important skills which can also be applied to your personal life. You learn how to speak (and listen) with empathy and patience. You can hone your skills in communication, flexibility, and reading body language. Physical strength can improve from helping others with daily tasks which in turn leads to greater health and well-being. You will likely learn about nutrition, human relationships, efficiency, mindfulness and you will gain knowledge of a plethora of medical terms. All these skills can serve you well in areas of your life outside of work. 3. You Model Generosity You may have a son or daughter, niece or nephew, or other young people in your life who look up to you. As a caregiver, you can show them how to be selfless and value others in their community. You are able to truly lead by example and demonstrate that caring for others is the right thing to do. 4. Insights About Aging If you are given the chance to care for an older adult, you can learn many things about the aging process. It may present you with new perspectives and ways to help prepare yourself or loved ones for that season of life. Not only can it give you a new outlook on how to help others. but it may also help you prioritize your goals and what matters to you. through a lens of gratitude, you will feel more fulfilled. This will translate into you becoming a more effective caregiver. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. articles.text: William (Bill) Howard passed away peacefully from cancer at home on November 17, 2022 surrounded by his family. Throughout his nearly two-year journey with glioblastoma, Bill never failed in his courtesy to his family and caregivers. He faced death with his usual grace. Born in San Francisco on October 1, 1950, he was the second child of Henry Howard, founder of the noted San Francisco law firm Howard, Rice, Nemerovski, Canady, Falk & Rabkin. He grew up just below Twin Peaks until the family moved to Hillsborough when he was six because his father was tired of San Francisco’s cold, foggy summers. Bill attended Stevenson School in Monterey and graduated from Burlingame High School. He studied theatre at the University of Seattle, and after graduation, Bill moved to New York City to pursue acting. He wrote to his mother that at 6’6” his one career obstacle was towering over other actors, giving casting directors a Bill Howard with sons Henry and Leland at Crater Lake, Oregon. Bill Howard died on November 17. He was 72. problem if they hired a short hero. He subsequently returned to San Francisco, where he earned his Master of Business Administration from Golden Gate University, and pursued a career in investment management, including managing HighMark Mutual Funds. During this time, Bill continued to pursue his passion in theatre through acting and directing productions in the Bohemian Club. Bill and his wife, Kyung Hee, moved to Piedmont in 1994 and raised two sons. Bill was present in his sons’ lives and enjoyed coaching their sports teams. He shared his love of the outdoors through backpacking and camping trips in the Sierra. Bill applied his woodworking talents in designing and building a beautiful home for his family. articles.text: It’s Thanksgiving morning, and Piedmont’s streets hold a charge of anticipation. 2,300 people stretch their legs and wish each other good luck, their breath forming white clouds in the air with every word in the crisp morning air. As the 8:30 a.m. start time approaches runners at Piedmont’s’ annual Turkey Trot stiffen and silence falls over the crowd. At the crack of starter’s gun , the 2022 Turkey Trot commences. Thousands of participants take off toward the finish line, five kilometers ahead of them. “It’s surreal seeing how many people are running alongside you,” said Piedmont High alum Ana Romanczuk, now a freshman at Chapman University. “I think [the number of runners] is inspiring and really pushes you to keep going and give it your all.” Piedmont’s annual Turkey Trot sees runners going solo as well as entire families completing the three-mile run together. Along the sidelines of the course, citizens set up stations with cups of water and apple juice to keep runners hydrated and refreshed. “People on the sidelines helped out, the firemen helped out, it really felt like the whole community came together to keep a tradition going,” Romanczuk said. Among the Turkey Trot’s challenges is the course itself, riddled with hills and steep climbs that enhance the challenge. “Magnolia hill was pretty hard. About a half-mile into the race it kind of hits you like a truck, and you aren’t quite warmed up yet. The Turkey Trot is notoriously very hilly,” PHS alum Jack Stein said. Piedmont’s natural hilly landscape is part of what gives the run its character and has Piedmonters preparing in the months in advance. “In my opinion Sea View was the hardest part of the run. The first part of the street is pretty brutal if you’re going for a fast time. It’s not a steep climb, but it’s a pretty long stretch uphill. It definitely felt good getting past that point,” said Xander Schulte-Sasse, a PHS junior on the Photo by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Piedmont Post intern Micah Temple reports on the Turkey Trot while running it. cross-country team. In the race, participants cheer each other on and encourage one another to push onward. “There’s not a super competitive or fierce attitude. Everybody just wants to motivate each other to go fast and not quit,” added PHS grad Charlie Lambert. Many of the Turkey Trot runners are current Piedmont residents, but with the race during Thanksgiving break, lots of college students come back home to participate. “My favorite part of the run has been coming back and seeing friends and family. I’ve been missing these guys in college, so it’s great to be able to come back and do something fun together,” Romanczuk said. Aside from the accomplishment runners get from undertaking an arduous endeavor such as the Turkey Trot, it brings Piedmonters and those coming from afar together on Thanksgiving day. “I’m happy to be here and home from college. Everyone comes out here on Thanksgiving morning. It’s a gathering spot where you can see everyone you’ve missed,’ said Stein. Micah Temple is a junior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post. He ran in this year’s Turkey Trot while taking notes for this story.
